sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Amanita muscaria has a scarlet to orange-red cap, convex when young and flattening with age, with irregular pale wart-like remains of the universal veil. Rain can remove the warts and fade the cap. Its crowded white to cream gills are free from the stem; the spore print is white. The white stem bears a broad hanging skirt-like ring and ends in a bulb with shaggy concentric belts of veil material, without a persistent deep sac.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: An ectomycorrhizal fungus growing on soil near tree partners, especially birch, pine and spruce. In Europe, fruiting bodies appear mainly from late summer through autumn; timing and size vary with site and weather.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: A rain-washed fly agaric can lose its white warts. Caesar’s mushroom (Amanita caesarea) can also have a red-orange cap, but its gills and stem are yellow and its volva is sack-like. The blusher (Amanita rubescens) stains pink to reddish when damaged. Never identify a mushroom by cap colour or an illustration alone: examine the whole stem base, gills and nearby trees.

sections.title: Toxicity
sections.text: Poisonous. Its principal neuroactive compounds are ibotenic acid and muscimol; poisoning belongs to the pantherina syndrome, distinct from the death cap’s amatoxin syndrome. Symptoms can begin about 30 minutes to 3 hours after ingestion and include nausea, vomiting, agitation, confusion, hallucinations or drowsiness. Severe cases can involve seizures, coma or respiratory complications; fatalities have been documented. Seek urgent poison-centre or emergency advice after suspected ingestion.

traits: Red to orange-red cap, up to about 20 cm, with removable pale veil warts
Crowded free white to cream gills and white spore print
White stem with a broad hanging ring
Bulbous base with concentric shaggy veil belts, not a deep sac-like volva
Mycorrhizal near birch, pine or spruce; mainly late summer to autumn
safetyNote: Poisonous: ibotenic acid and muscimol can cause digestive and neuropsychiatric symptoms about 30 minutes to 3 hours after ingestion; severe poisoning is possible. Do not eat. If ingestion is suspected, contact a poison centre or emergency service promptly.
